newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy to delay Stet sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Italy to delay Stet sell-off.

text.p: Italy said on Monday it wanted to merge the state telecommunications holding company Stet with its operating arm Telecom Italia but that privatisation of the merged entity would have to wait until late 1997.
The government had wanted to privatise Stet, which holds a controlling stake in Telecom Italia, by the end of March 1997.

The Treasury said in a statement after Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi met Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert in Brussels that parliamentary delay in creating a telecoms watchdog to police the sector made the move inevitable.
Ciampi ordered state holding IRI, which owns 64 percent of Stet ordinary stock, to merge the telecom holding with telephone operating unit Telecom Italia, the statement said.
"The present stage of the parliamentary debate...rules out a possibility to privatise by March 1997," the statement quoted Ciampi as saying. Stet was due to have been sold by next March 31.
"Realistically this has to be postponed to the autumn of 1997," it said.

Industry analysts said the delay meant Stet now had to take its place in the European telecoms privatisations queue behind Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom, due this month and next summer respectively.

The statement said Van Miert was deeply disappointed that the sale of Stet, Europe's fourth-biggest telephone concern, would not go ahead on time but Italy's centre-left government put a brave face on the delay.
Government undersecretary Enrico Micheli said the merger of Stet and Telecom Italia, which it controls, would boost the attractiveness of the stock and lift proceeds for the Treasury.

Stet shares rose sharply on the prospect of losing the "holding company" tag which had weighed on its shares, to finish up 6.18 percent at 5,674 lire. Telecom Italia Mobile (TIM), its mobile phone group, gained 2.54 percent to 3,313 lire.

Stet, which is listed on the Milan bourse, currently trades at a big discount to the value of the assets it controls, something which analysts believe could discourage overseas investors from buying the stock when it is privatised.
"Having a box which contained the others was an Italian anomaly. (The merger) means helping the privatisation and containing the holding's discount," said Enrico Micheli.
But Telecom Italia's fell 7.85 percent to 3,321 lire because it now will be be seen just as another part of Stet.
The offering of Stet was to have been Italy's next big privatisation, following hot closely on the successful sale of a second tranche of energy giant ENI last month.

The government has also been under pressure to sell Stet speedily to stave off bankruptcy at IRI, the state monolith set up by Fascist dictator Benito Mussolini which faces a loss of up to three trillion lire ($2 billion) in 1996.
Under a 1993 accord with the European Union, IRI must also chop its debt to below five trillion lire by the year-end from its end-1995 level of 22.5 trillion.

The statement said Van Miert had agreed that Stet shares should be transferred to the Treasury from IRI, which would also take up some of IRI's debt, to ease IRI's precarious finances during the transition to the Stet sale.
Van Miert said earlier this month the Italian government's credibility was on the line over the Stet sale and IRI debt reduction.

But a key government ally, the hardline Communist Refoundation party, is ideologically opposed to the sell-off and has presented hundreds of amendments to the telecoms watchdog bill in a bid to scupper its progress.
"The problem of the (telecom) authority remains," Micheli said.
